children: The world's largest cold-storage operator by capacity is suing a solar-panel provider and a contractor, alleging their negligence caused a fire that destroyed a Los Angeles warehouse.

Lineage filed suit Thursday in Los Angeles Superior Court against Altus Power, which is owned by private-equity firm TPG, and Pearce Services, a subsidiary of commercial real-estate company CBRE Group.

The fire started June 17 at the 500,000-square-foot, temperature-controlled warehouse in the Boyle Heights neighborhood and smoldered for days. The building was storing millions of pounds of fresh and frozen food such as meat, bread and seafood that rotted after the blaze, prompting complaints, citations and lawsuits over foul odors and pests.

Los Palos Street Operating, a subsidiary of Altus, leased the building's roof from Lineage to own and operate a solar-panel array. The suit contends Los Palos hired Pearce to conduct maintenance on the panels and the fire started while Pearce employees were working on the array.
Los Palos refuted Lineage's claims and said it plans to contest the accusations in court.
"Lineage's statement is riddled with misinformation in a blatant attempt to deflect blame for their role in this matter," a company representative said.

"We take safety extremely seriously and our strong safety record reflects our rigorous protocols and response procedures," the representative said. "Lineage is legally responsible for overseeing the site remediation, including cleanup, debris removal and remediation resources."

A spokesperson for Pearce said the company disputes Lineage's allegations that Pearce caused the fire. "Investigation into the fire's cause, origin and reasons for its spread remains ongoing, and it is premature for anyone to draw conclusions," the spokesperson said. "Pearce looks forward to vigorously defending itself against these allegations through the legal process."

Lineage is seeking compensation for estimated damages of more than $1 billion from the fire. That includes property and reputational damage, cleanup expenses and lawsuits filed by neighborhood residents alleging health and air-quality concerns.

The suit alleges Altus and Pearce didn't help with site cleanup or community assistance in the wake of the fire. It also says the rooftop solar-panel array had previously sparked a smaller fire in August 2024.

Many warehouse operators and other commercial real-estate owners have installed solar panels on building roofs over the past decade. The technology is seen as a way to cut energy costs, reduce emissions and at times make money from what is typically largely empty space.
But there are risks involved. Walmart in 2019 sued Tesla, alleging some of the company's solar panels sparked fires on the roofs of several stores. The companies settled the suit months later.
